pull.title: KAFKA-20665: Report the end offset of a warm-up task with nothing to restore
pull.body:
A standby task, and so a warm-up task, learned the end offset of a
changelog only from a restored batch. With nothing to restore -- an
empty changelog, or local state already at the end of an idle changelog
-- no batch ever arrives. The client then kept reporting an end offset
of Long.MAX_VALUE for the task, which the broker reads as an unknown
lag. The warm-up task therefore never counted as caught up, and its
migration stayed staged forever, holding a warm-up slot.

When the restore consumer of a standby task reports a lag of 0 for a
changelog without a restore end offset, the changelog reader now also
records the end offset, as the last offset like a restored batch does:
-1 for an empty changelog.

The reported end offset of such a changelog is now one past that last
offset, the next offset to fetch, as for the restore end offset of an
active task or of a source-topic changelog. A negative end offset would
otherwise be summed into Long.MAX_VALUE, and reach custom assignors
through the assignor API. A fully restored standby task now reports a
lag of 0 instead of -1 per changelog.

issue.title: KAFKA-20665: Report active task restore progress the broker acts on

repository.name: kafka
repository.description: Apache Kafka - A distributed event streaming platform

issue.body:
A client reports the changelog offsets of an active task only while it
restores the task. The heartbeat carries offsets only when the
assignment changes, when streams.task.offset.interval.ms passes (default
60 s), or when a warm-up task is within acceptable.recovery.lag. So the
broker learned that an active task had finished restoring, or had come
within acceptable.recovery.lag, only with the next periodic report.
Until then the refiner took the owner to be restoring the task with an
old lag. It did not protect the owner as hot, and it granted a migration
off that owner cold instead of staging it behind a warm-up task.

The client now also sends offsets on the next heartbeat when an active
task it restores comes within acceptable.recovery.lag, and when an
active task that was in the last sent offsets has dropped out of them,
ie, finished restoring. The warm-up and active checks share one
predicate.

The refiner can still run on another member's heartbeat before the
member that finished restoring has sent its offsets. That window is now
at most one heartbeat interval, instead of the task offset interval.
